# Example configs

<!-- Generated by tools/gen_config_gallery.py from the files in configs/. Do not edit
     by hand: change the config's header comment and regenerate. -->

Every sweep is one YAML file: the machines (`devices`), the model files (`models`),
and a `matrix` that expands into concrete runs. Preview any of them without running
anything:

```
mlsys run <config> --dry-run
```

**Templates** are written to be copied. Each has `# <-- EDIT` markers on the lines
that name your paths, and a header that says what to run before and after.

**Studies** are the exact configs behind the shipped datasets and write-ups, kept so a
result can be traced to the sweep that produced it. Their paths point at the author's
machines; use them as worked examples, or edit the device and model blocks to repeat
a study on your own hardware.

The counts below come from expanding each file with the same loader `mlsys run` uses.

### onnx-cpu.yaml

ONNX Runtime on the CPU: latency percentiles and batch scaling for one model.

The onnxruntime backend times inference in-process on the device and reports mean, p50, p95 and p99 latency plus throughput, at each batch size. It needs onnxruntime in the interpreter the device points at (`pip install ml-systems-lab[onnx]` covers the local one); `python:` lets a device use a different environment from the harness.

Which quantization of one model decodes fastest on this machine?

### sbc-over-ssh.yaml

Benchmark a single-board computer from your laptop, over SSH.

The agent is copied to the board as source and runs there under the board's own Python (3.9 or newer, standard library only), so nothing is installed on the device and no network round trip sits inside a measurement. On a Raspberry Pi 5 the record also carries per-rail PMIC power, temperature and the throttle bits.

### thread-scaling.yaml

Where does decode stop scaling with threads on this CPU?

Decode is memory-bound, so throughput climbs with threads until the memory system is saturated and then flattens. On hybrid CPUs (performance plus efficiency cores) it can keep rising past the performance-core count, and past the peak the run-to-run spread widens sharply. Two model sizes and a fine thread sweep show where the peak sits.

| | |
|---|---|
| file | [`configs/examples/thread-scaling.yaml`](https://github.com/manunicholasjacob/ml-systems-lab/blob/main/configs/examples/thread-scaling.yaml) |
| experiment | `thread-scaling` |
| devices | `local` (local) |
| backend / mode | llamacpp / throughput |
| runs | 14 |

```
mlsys run configs/examples/thread-scaling.yaml --dry-run
```

### ttft-latency.yaml

How long does a user wait for the first token, and how does that grow with the prompt?

Latency mode drives llama-server over its streaming API and times the first chunk (TTFT) and the last one (end-to-end), which is what an interactive user experiences. llama-bench measures neither. TTFT is mostly prefill, so it grows close to linearly with prompt length; this sweep shows the slope on your hardware.

| | |
|---|---|
| file | [`configs/examples/ttft-latency.yaml`](https://github.com/manunicholasjacob/ml-systems-lab/blob/main/configs/examples/ttft-latency.yaml) |
| experiment | `ttft-latency` |
| devices | `local` (local) |
| backend / mode | llamacpp / latency |
| runs | 3 |

```
mlsys run configs/examples/ttft-latency.yaml --dry-run
```

### two-machines.yaml

One sweep across two machines at once: a laptop and a board over SSH.

With --concurrent the scheduler runs each device's queue in parallel, subject to each device's max_concurrency, so the sweep takes about as long as the slower machine rather than the sum of both. A clock check runs first and its offset is recorded. Only transport failures (a dropped SSH connection) are retried; a model that does not fit is a result, not a retry.

| | |
|---|---|
| file | [`configs/examples/two-machines.yaml`](https://github.com/manunicholasjacob/ml-systems-lab/blob/main/configs/examples/two-machines.yaml) |
| experiment | `two-machines` |
| devices | `laptop` (local), `sbc` (ssh) |
| backend / mode | llamacpp / throughput |
| runs | 6 |

```
mlsys run configs/examples/two-machines.yaml --dry-run
```

### cluster.yaml

Three genuinely different machines, one sweep, run at once.

This is the config that demonstrates the scheduler, as opposed to the containerisation study in configs/containerization.yaml, which deliberately arranges for the arms *not* to overlap because they share a CPU. Here they do not share anything, so they overlap, and the sweep takes about as long as its slowest device rather than the sum of all of them.

### int8-anomaly.yaml

Falsification study for the cross-ISA int8 observation.

Observed in the August 2026 campaigns on CIFAR-sized (32x32) inputs: int8 ResNet18 ran faster than fp32 on the Cortex-A76 and slower than fp32 on the i7-12700H, in the same runtime family. Treat that as an observation to be falsified, not as a result.

### pi-overnight.yaml

The full Pi 5 matrix. Spec coverage: 3 model sizes, 5 quantisations, thread sweep, prompt/output length sweeps, context-depth sweep, TTFT latency mode, ONNX Runtime as the second backend, and power measured in separate runs per the two-run rule.

Blocks are ordered smallest-model-first so an early failure costs the least, and every llama.cpp point resets swap and drops caches: on a 2 GB board, resident pages from the previous model turn the next run into an SD-card streaming benchmark.

### thread-cliff.yaml

Hypothesis: On Alder Lake hybrid CPUs (6P + 8E cores), LLM decode throughput peaks at the P-core count and collapses beyond it, with the magnitude of collapse inversely proportional to model size.

The i7-12700H has 6 P-cores (3.5-4.7 GHz, large L2) and 8 E-cores (2.3-3.5 GHz, shared L2). At t<=6, only P-cores are scheduled. At t>6, E-cores mix in. Decode is bandwidth-bound (matrix-vector); prefill is compute-bound (matrix-matrix). E-cores have lower IPC and smaller caches, which should hurt decode more than prefill.

| | |
|---|---|
| file | [`configs/thread-cliff.yaml`](https://github.com/manunicholasjacob/ml-systems-lab/blob/main/configs/thread-cliff.yaml) |
| experiment | `thread-cliff` |
| devices | `laptop` (local) |
| backend / mode | llamacpp / throughput |
| runs | 33 |

```
mlsys run configs/thread-cliff.yaml --dry-run
```

## Adding one

A config that answers a question other people ask is welcome as a pull request.
Put a template in `configs/examples/`, open it with a header comment whose first
paragraph says what question it answers, mark every machine-specific line with
`# <-- EDIT`, and run `python tools/gen_config_gallery.py` to add it here.
